lesson.title: Fire and Forget: What Makes Something a Datagram
lesson.summary: A datagram is a self-contained unit of data that can be routed to its destination independently, with no connection setup and no guarantee of delivery, and the term applies both to UDP's transport-layer messages and, historically, to IP itself.
lesson.body:
A TCP segment, from the previous chapter, belongs to an ongoing, stateful conversation, tracked by sequence numbers, between two endpoints that first shook hands to open a connection. A datagram is the opposite idea. It is a self-contained unit of data that carries enough addressing information to be routed from source to destination entirely on its own, with no requirement that the sender and receiver establish any connection beforehand, and no guarantee from the network that it will arrive, arrive exactly once, or arrive in the order it was sent. Where a segment is one numbered piece of a larger, tracked stream, a datagram simply stands alone.

This term shows up at two different layers in networking, and both usages are legitimate. At the transport layer, UDP, the User Datagram Protocol, defined in RFC 768 back in 1980, explicitly names its own unit of data a datagram: a compact 8-byte header holding a source port, destination port, length, and checksum, attached to a payload, with no handshake, no sequence numbers, and no built-in retransmission of any kind. Separately, and earlier historically, IP itself was described using the same word. RFC 791, which defines IP, describes its job as delivering internet datagrams from a source host to a destination host on a connectionless, best-effort basis, which is exactly why what the earlier Packet chapter called an IP packet is still occasionally called a datagram in more formal or older material, even though packet is by far the more common everyday term today.

A DNS lookup is a clean, concrete example of the datagram model in action. When your laptop resolves a domain name, it typically sends a single UDP datagram to a DNS server on port 53, containing one question: what is the IP address for a given hostname. The server sends back a single UDP datagram containing the answer. There is no handshake beforehand, no persistent connection state kept on either side, and no sequence number linking this exchange to any other query. If the datagram carrying the answer is lost in transit, the resolver simply notices it never got a reply, waits out a timeout, and sends an entirely new, independent datagram to try again, rather than TCP's approach of noticing one specific numbered gap and retransmitting only the missing bytes.

This tradeoff, no reliability guarantee in exchange for far less overhead, is deliberate rather than a shortcoming. Skipping the handshake and the per-connection state a server would otherwise track makes UDP well suited to small, one-shot transactions like DNS lookups, where the cost of trying again is lower than the cost of setting up and tearing down a full connection. It also suits real-time voice or video calls, where a segment arriving late after retransmission is often more disruptive than a dropped one being silently skipped. Applications that need reliability on top of UDP, and some do, have to build it themselves, which is exactly the job TCP already does for anyone willing to use its segment-based, connection-oriented model instead.

Across these last four chapters, one path from application data down to the physical wire, and back up again, is now complete: a byte is the basic unit of measurement, a frame carries data across one physical hop, a packet carries data across many hops, and at the top, a segment or a datagram carries data between two applications, either as a tracked, reliable stream or as an independent, connectionless message, depending on what the application actually needs.
